<!-- Generated from why-bootstrap.Rmd.orig by precompute/precompile.R. Edit the .orig file, not this one. -->



Sensitivity analysis asks how strong an omitted variable would have to be
to change a regression result. The most common answer in management
research is the impact threshold of a confounding variable (ITCV; Frank,
2000): the smallest product of correlations with the predictor and with the
outcome that an omitted variable needs to make a significant coefficient
insignificant. `sensemakr` (Cinelli & Hazlett, 2020) answers differently: it
reports the coefficient you would have obtained had a variable as strong as
an observed covariate been omitted, with a confidence interval.

Lonati and Wulff (2026) show that both answers rest on the conventional OLS
variance formula. The ITCV is computed from a *t* statistic, and its reading
as a product of correlations holds only when that *t* statistic is the
conventional one. The confidence interval of `sensemakr` is derived under the
same assumption. As soon as the regression calls for heteroskedasticity- or
cluster-robust standard errors, which is the rule rather than the exception
in organizational research, the ITCV remains computable but is no longer a
product of correlations, and the analytic interval is wrong by the same
factor as the conventional standard error. The remedy is to bootstrap
`sensemakr`, as Cinelli, Ferwerda and Hazlett (2024, Appendix C) propose;
`bootmakr` automates it.

This page shows the problem and the remedy on the package's simulated data,
in R and in Stata.

## The example

`firms` is a simulated panel of 250 firms observed for 20 years. The true
effect of `x` on `y` is 0.25. Two firm-level characteristics drive both `x`
and `y`: an observed control `c` and a variable `q` that we leave out of the
regression, as a researcher who does not have it would. The within-firm
components of `x` and of the disturbance are persistent, so standard errors
must be clustered by firm. Because the data are simulated, `q` is in the
file and every verdict can be checked.

## One coefficient, two standard errors

Estimate the regression that omits `q`, once with conventional and once with
cluster-robust standard errors.

<div class="tab-content">
<div class="tab-pane active" id="se-r" role="tabpanel" aria-labelledby="se-r-tab">


``` r
library(bootmakr)
library(sandwich)
data("firms")

fit <- lm(y ~ x + c, data = firms)

se <- c(conventional = sqrt(vcov(fit)["x", "x"]),
        clustered    = sqrt(vcovCL(fit, cluster = ~ firm)["x", "x"]))
round(c(estimate = coef(fit)[["x"]], se, ratio = se[["clustered"]] / se[["conventional"]]), 3)
#>     estimate conventional    clustered        ratio 
#>        0.445        0.014        0.041        2.984
```

</div>
<div class="tab-pane" id="se-stata" role="tabpanel" aria-labelledby="se-stata-tab">

```stata
use firms, clear
```

```stata
quietly regress y x c
lincom x

quietly regress y x c, vce(cluster firm)
lincom x
```

```{.stata-output}

------------------------------------------------------------------------------

-------------+----------------------------------------------------------------
         (1) |   .4445283    .013584    32.72   0.000     .4178977    .4711589
------------------------------------------------------------------------------

 ( 1)  x = 0

------------------------------------------------------------------------------

-------------+----------------------------------------------------------------

```

</div>

The coefficient is 0.44, well above the true 0.25, because `q` is
omitted. The clustered standard error is 3.0 times the
conventional one. Nothing about the coefficient changed; only the
uncertainty attached to it did.

## What the ITCV makes of it

The ITCV turns the *t* statistic of the coefficient into a *t*-implied
correlation, *t* / √(*t*² + df), does the same for the critical *t*, and
reports the gap between the two, rescaled so that it reads as the product of
correlations an omitted variable would need to close it. Here it is for both
*t* statistics. (The code implements the definition directly; the `konfound`
packages for R and Stata give the same numbers.)

<div class="lang-tabs">
<ul class="nav nav-tabs" role="tablist">
<li class="nav-item" role="presentation"><button class="nav-link active" id="itcv-r-tab" data-bs-toggle="tab" data-bs-target="#itcv-r" type="button" role="tab" aria-controls="itcv-r" aria-selected="true" data-lang="r">R</button></li>
<li class="nav-item" role="presentation"><button class="nav-link" id="itcv-stata-tab" data-bs-toggle="tab" data-bs-target="#itcv-stata" type="button" role="tab" aria-controls="itcv-stata" aria-selected="false" data-lang="stata">Stata</button></li>
</ul>
<div class="tab-content">
<div class="tab-pane active" id="itcv-r" role="tabpanel" aria-labelledby="itcv-r-tab">


``` r
t.conv <- coef(fit)[["x"]] / se[["conventional"]]
t.clus <- coef(fit)[["x"]] / se[["clustered"]]
df <- fit$df.residual

itcv <- function(t, df) {
  r.implied  <- t / sqrt(t^2 + df)             # the t-implied correlation
  t.crit     <- qt(0.975, df)
  r.critical <- t.crit / sqrt(t.crit^2 + df)
  c(r_implied = r.implied, ITCV = (r.implied - r.critical) / (1 - abs(r.critical)))
}
round(rbind(conventional = itcv(t.conv, df), clustered = itcv(t.clus, df)), 3)
#>              r_implied  ITCV
#> conventional     0.420 0.404
#> clustered        0.153 0.129
```

</div>
<div class="tab-pane" id="itcv-stata" role="tabpanel" aria-labelledby="itcv-stata-tab">

```stata
quietly regress y x c
scalar t_conv = _b[x] / _se[x]
scalar df = e(df_r)
quietly regress y x c, vce(cluster firm)
scalar t_rob = _b[x] / _se[x]

* the ITCV: t-implied correlation minus the critical one (Frank, 2000)
scalar r_crit = invttail(df, .025) / sqrt(invttail(df, .025)^2 + df)
foreach v in conv rob {
    scalar r_impl_`v' = t_`v' / sqrt(t_`v'^2 + df)
    scalar itcv_`v' = (r_impl_`v' - r_crit) / (1 - abs(r_crit))
}
display "conventional SE: t-implied correlation = " %5.3f r_impl_conv ///
    "   ITCV = " %5.3f itcv_conv
display "clustered SE:    t-implied correlation = " %5.3f r_impl_rob ///
    "   ITCV = " %5.3f itcv_rob "   sqrt(ITCV) = " %5.3f sqrt(itcv_rob)
```

```{.stata-output}
conventional SE: t-implied correlation = 0.420   ITCV = 0.404

clustered SE:    t-implied correlation = 0.153   ITCV = 0.129   sqrt(ITCV) = 0.359
```

</div>
</div>
</div>



With conventional standard errors the ITCV is
.40; with clustered ones it drops to
.13. Read as a product of
correlations, the second number says that an omitted variable correlated
about .36 with both `x` and `y`
(the square root of the ITCV) would be enough to overturn the result. Now
look at `q`, whose correlations we know. The ITCV is stated in correlations
given the other covariates, so we take `q`'s partial correlations given `c`.

<div class="lang-tabs">
<ul class="nav nav-tabs" role="tablist">
<li class="nav-item" role="presentation"><button class="nav-link active" id="impact-r-tab" data-bs-toggle="tab" data-bs-target="#impact-r" type="button" role="tab" aria-controls="impact-r" aria-selected="true" data-lang="r">R</button></li>
<li class="nav-item" role="presentation"><button class="nav-link" id="impact-stata-tab" data-bs-toggle="tab" data-bs-target="#impact-stata" type="button" role="tab" aria-controls="impact-stata" aria-selected="false" data-lang="stata">Stata</button></li>
</ul>
<div class="tab-content">
<div class="tab-pane active" id="impact-r" role="tabpanel" aria-labelledby="impact-r-tab">


``` r
partial <- function(a, b) {
  cor(resid(lm(firms[[a]] ~ firms$c)), resid(lm(firms[[b]] ~ firms$c)))
}
round(c(q_with_x = partial("q", "x"), q_with_y = partial("q", "y"),
        impact = partial("q", "x") * partial("q", "y"),
        x_with_y = partial("x", "y")), 3)
#> q_with_x q_with_y   impact x_with_y 
#>    0.468    0.537    0.251    0.420
```

</div>
<div class="tab-pane" id="impact-stata" role="tabpanel" aria-labelledby="impact-stata-tab">

```stata
* partial correlations given c, by residualising on c
foreach v in x y q {
    quietly regress `v' c
    predict double `v'_c, resid
}
quietly correlate x_c y_c
scalar r_xy_c = r(rho)
quietly correlate x_c q_c
scalar r_xq_c = r(rho)
quietly correlate y_c q_c
scalar r_yq_c = r(rho)
display "partial correlation of x and y given c: " %5.3f r_xy_c
display "q with x given c: " %5.3f r_xq_c "   q with y given c: " %5.3f r_yq_c ///
    "   impact of q: " %5.3f r_xq_c * r_yq_c
```

```{.stata-output}
partial correlation of x and y given c: 0.420

q with x given c: 0.468   q with y given c: 0.537   impact of q: 0.251
```

</div>
</div>
</div>



The impact of `q` is .25. That is below the
conventional ITCV (.40), so the
conventional ITCV says that `q` is *not* strong enough to overturn the
result. It is above the clustered ITCV
(.13), so the clustered ITCV says
that `q` *is* strong enough. One of them must be wrong, and we can find out
which: put `q` into the regression.

<div class="lang-tabs">
<ul class="nav nav-tabs" role="tablist">
<li class="nav-item" role="presentation"><button class="nav-link active" id="withq-r-tab" data-bs-toggle="tab" data-bs-target="#withq-r" type="button" role="tab" aria-controls="withq-r" aria-selected="true" data-lang="r">R</button></li>

</ul>
<div class="tab-content">
<div class="tab-pane active" id="withq-r" role="tabpanel" aria-labelledby="withq-r-tab">


``` r
fit.q <- lm(y ~ x + c + q, data = firms)
round(c(estimate = coef(fit.q)[["x"]],
        se_conventional = sqrt(vcov(fit.q)["x", "x"]),
        se_clustered    = sqrt(vcovCL(fit.q, cluster = ~ firm)["x", "x"])), 3)
#>        estimate se_conventional    se_clustered 
#>           0.229           0.014           0.037
```

</div>
<div class="tab-pane" id="withq-stata" role="tabpanel" aria-labelledby="withq-stata-tab">

```stata
regress y x c q, vce(cluster firm)
```

With `q` in the model the coefficient of `x` is 0.23, close to the
true 0.25, with a clustered standard error of 0.037: it remains
clearly different from zero. The clustered ITCV was wrong. Its reading as a
product of correlations fails because the *t*-implied correlation it is
built on, .15, is not the
correlation between `x` and `y` given `c`, which is
.42. With conventional standard errors the two
coincide (.42); that
coincidence is what the ITCV derivation uses. With robust standard errors
the *t*-implied correlation equals the actual correlation divided by
√(ratio² (1 − *r*²) + *r*²), where ratio is the robust standard error over
the conventional one (Lonati & Wulff, 2026, Equation 4). When robust standard
errors are larger than conventional ones, the usual case, the ITCV
overstates the threat from omitted variables; when they are smaller, it
understates it. There is no "correct ITCV" to be had under robust inference:
two omitted variables with the same correlations can change a robust
standard error in different ways, so no product of correlations corresponds
to the robust *t* statistic. Degrees-of-freedom corrections, fixed effects
and feasible generalized least squares do not repair this; the paper goes
through each of them.

## Analytic sensemakr has the same problem

`sensemakr` does not need the ITCV. For an omitted variable as strong as
`c`, it computes the bias-adjusted coefficient directly, and that estimate
is a function of the data alone. But the standard error and confidence
interval it attaches to the adjusted coefficient are derived under
conventional OLS inference (Cinelli & Hazlett, 2020, Section 4.3).

#>   bound_label adjusted_estimate adjusted_se adjusted_lower_CI adjusted_upper_CI

The adjusted estimate, 0.252, is close to the
coefficient with `q` in the model. Its analytic standard error,
0.013, is close to the *conventional* standard error of
that coefficient (0.014) and far below the clustered one
(0.037). The analytic interval, from
0.226 to 0.278, is
therefore about 2.8 times too narrow in
these data, for exactly the reason the ITCV fails: a formula built on the
conventional variance is being applied to a regression that needs a robust
one.

## What the bootstrap does

Cinelli, Ferwerda and Hazlett (2024, Appendix C) propose to replace the
analytic interval by a bootstrap: resample the data the way you would choose
standard errors (observations for heteroskedasticity, whole clusters for
clustered data), refit the regression and recompute the adjusted estimate in
every replication, and take the percentiles of the resulting distribution as
the confidence interval. `bootmakr` does this in one call.

<div class="lang-tabs">
<ul class="nav nav-tabs" role="tablist">
<li class="nav-item" role="presentation"><button class="nav-link active" id="boot-r-tab" data-bs-toggle="tab" data-bs-target="#boot-r" type="button" role="tab" aria-controls="boot-r" aria-selected="true" data-lang="r">R</button></li>
<li class="nav-item" role="presentation"><button class="nav-link" id="boot-stata-tab" data-bs-toggle="tab" data-bs-target="#boot-stata" type="button" role="tab" aria-controls="boot-stata" aria-selected="false" data-lang="stata">Stata</button></li>
</ul>
<div class="tab-content">
<div class="tab-pane active" id="boot-r" role="tabpanel" aria-labelledby="boot-r-tab">


``` r
boot <- bootmakr(y ~ x + c, data = firms, treat = "x",
                 benchmark_covariates = "c", cluster = "firm",
                 seed = 123, progress = FALSE)
boot
#> 
#> Call:
#> bootmakr(formula = y ~ x + c, data = firms, treat = "x", benchmark_covariates = "c", 
#>     seed = 123, cluster = "firm", progress = FALSE)
#> 
#> Bootstrap sensitivity analysis (1,000 reps, n = 5,000, 250 clusters)
#> Benchmark: c | kd = 1, ky = 1
#> 
#> Adjusted estimates (percentile 95% CI):
#>   Estimate Std. Err     2.5%    97.5% Pr(>|0|)  
#> x 0.252134 0.076236 0.087365 0.394215     0.01 *
#> ---
#> Signif. codes:  0 '***' 0.001 '**' 0.01 '*' 0.05 '.' 0.1 ' ' 1
#> (H0: adjusted estimate = 0; CI and p-value from percentile bootstrap)
#> 
#> Benchmark strength (descriptive: computed from the data, no standard errors involved)
#>                       Partial R2 |Partial r|
#> c with treatment | X      0.1433       0.379
#> c with outcome | D, X     0.1248       0.353
#> Implied strength of the omitted variable (sensemakr bounds):
#>           kd   ky R2dz.x R2yz.dx Impact
#> 1.00x c 1.00 1.00 0.1673  0.1998  0.222
#> (R2dz.x, R2yz.dx: partial R2 of the omitted variable with the treatment given the
#>  covariates, and with the outcome given treatment and covariates. Impact: product of
#>  its partial correlations with the outcome and with the treatment, both given the
#>  covariates only, i.e. the scale of the ITCV; signed so that the omitted variable
#>  biases the estimate away from zero. Descriptive only: independent of the variance
#>  estimator, and not a threshold.)
```

The adjusted estimate is the same as before. Its bootstrap standard error is
0.076 (0.074 in Stata, which draws different random
numbers), and the percentile interval runs from 0.09 to
0.39. The interval is wider than the clustered interval of
the regression that includes `q`, for two reasons. One is the reason this
page is about: the bootstrap, resampling firms, reflects the clustered
uncertainty of the coefficient, not the conventional one. The other is that
in every replication the strength of the benchmark `c` is re-estimated too,
so the interval also carries the uncertainty about how strong "as strong as
`c`" is. The paper's own example (Table 2 of Lonati & Wulff, 2026) separates
the two by giving `sensemakr` the omitted variable's strength directly,
which the R package allows:


``` r
manual <- bootmakr(y ~ x + c, data = firms, treat = "x",
                   r2dz.x  = partial("q", "x")^2,
                   r2yz.dx = sensemakr::partial_r2(fit.q, covariates = "q"),
                   cluster = "firm", seed = 123, progress = FALSE)
manual$results[, c("estimate", "se", "ci_lower", "ci_upper", "pvalue")]
#>    estimate         se  ci_lower  ci_upper pvalue
#> 1 0.2286068 0.04087705 0.1511528 0.3088602      0
```



With `q`'s actual strength, the bootstrap standard error is
0.041, next to the clustered standard error of 0.037
that the regression with `q` gives: the bootstrap recovers the inference
that would have been obtained had `q` been observed, as it does in the
paper. (The `sensemakr` command on SSC does not accept a strength given by
hand, so this step has no Stata counterpart.)

The resampling scheme is what makes the bootstrap robust, and it is your
choice. Resampling observations instead of firms gives

<div class="tab-pane active" id="rows-r" role="tabpanel" aria-labelledby="rows-r-tab">


``` r
rows <- bootmakr(y ~ x + c, data = firms, treat = "x",
                 benchmark_covariates = "c",
                 seed = 123, progress = FALSE)
rows$results[, c("estimate", "se", "ci_lower", "ci_upper")]
#>    estimate         se ci_lower ci_upper
#> 1 0.2521337 0.02115902 0.211228 0.295048
```

</div>
<div class="tab-pane" id="rows-stata" role="tabpanel" aria-labelledby="rows-stata-tab">

```stata
quietly bootmakr y x c, treat(x) benchmark(c) seed(123)
display "observations resampled:  SE = " %6.4f r(se) ///
    "   95% CI [" %6.4f r(ci_lower) ", " %6.4f r(ci_upper) "]"
```

```{.stata-output}
observations resampled:  SE = 0.0216   95% CI [0.2078, 0.2937]
```

</div>
</div>
</div>



a standard error of 0.021, too small by the same factor as the
conventional standard error, because observations of the same firm are
treated as independent. Resample the units you would cluster on; see
[Clustered and stratified data](clustering.html).

## In the paper

Lonati and Wulff (2026) make this argument formally, illustrate it with a
simulated example like the one above (without `c`, and with a stronger `q`),
and test bootstrap-based `sensemakr` against the ITCV in a Monte Carlo study
with heteroskedastic, clustered, unbalanced and weak-benchmark designs. The
bootstrap interval comes close to nominal coverage throughout, while the
ITCV's mistakes grow with the sample size under clustering. The paper ends
with a four-stage workflow (which standard errors, how different are they,
how strong is a plausible omitted variable, can the bootstrap be trusted)
that the [worked example](ceo-pay.html) follows on a published study.
